markets.title: What is a prediction market?
markets.blurb: A place where people trade on whether something will happen.
simple: A prediction market asks a question with a yes-or-no answer that will be settled later: will it rain in London on Friday, will this team win on Sunday.
People buy and sell shares in each answer. A share of the answer that turns out right pays one dollar; a share of the wrong answer pays nothing.
Because a right share pays a dollar, the price of a share is what traders together think the chance is. A share at 62 cents is the market saying 62% chance.
Here you do not trade real money. You watch strategies make forecasts and trade with play money, and see how they would have done in the past.
detailed: A binary contract on event A pays 1 if A occurs and 0 otherwise. Its price q in (0, 1) is the market-implied probability of A, up to the spread and fees.
Every market here has exactly two outcomes, and the first outcome is the event forecast: “Yes” for a yes/no question, the first-named side otherwise. Forecasts, prices and labels all refer to it.
A market's label is set only from the venue's settlement, never from a price: a market that has stopped trading is not yet resolved.

price.title: Why the price is a forecast
price.blurb: A market's price is a chance, and usually a good one.
simple: If a share paying a dollar costs 62 cents, anyone who thought the true chance was higher could expect to profit by buying, and anyone who thought it lower by selling. The price settles where those views balance.
That makes the price a forecast, and often a hard one to beat: it pools what many people know and they put money behind it.
Every strategy here is measured against the market's own price. Beating it is the test; matching it is what you get for doing nothing.
detailed: Forecasts are scored with the Brier score, the mean of (p − y)² over settled markets, where p is the forecast and y is 1 if the event happened. Lower is better; always saying 0.5 scores 0.25.
Skill against the market is 1 − Brier(strategy) / Brier(market) on the same markets. Positive means the strategy forecast better than the price; the market's own skill is 0 by definition.
The Brier score is strictly proper: a forecaster minimises its expected score only by reporting what it believes, so it cannot be gamed by shading forecasts.
refs: Brier, G. W. (1950). Verification of forecasts expressed in terms of probability. Monthly Weather Review 78(1), 1–3.
Gneiting, T. and Raftery, A. E. (2007). Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation. JASA 102(477), 359–378.

backtest.title: What a backtest is, and is not
backtest.blurb: Replaying the past to see how a strategy would have done.
simple: A backtest takes markets that have already settled, goes back to a moment before they settled (the cutoff), and asks a strategy for its forecast using only what was known then.
It then pretends to bet on those forecasts and adds up how the bets would have turned out. That gives a score and a play-money result.

A backtest is not a promise. A strategy that did well on a few dozen markets may have been lucky, and one that had seen the answers, even by accident, will look better than it is. This is why every strategy here is also run forward, on markets that have not settled yet.
detailed: Every forecaster takes an explicit information cutoff and must not read anything after it; the backtest places it a fixed number of hours before each market settled.

A claim of skill needs enough markets. Detecting a mean Brier edge δ at 5% with 80% power needs about 7.85 σ²/δ² settled markets, where σ is the spread of the per-market difference; with σ near 0.13 a two-point edge needs about 350.
A language model may already know how any market that resolved before its training cutoff turned out, so its backtest counts as evidence only on markets that resolved after that date.
refs: Murphy, A. H. (1973). A new vector partition of the probability score. Journal of Applied Meteorology 12(4), 595–600.

paper.title: Paper trading
paper.blurb: Trading with play money on markets that have not settled yet.
simple: Paper trading runs a strategy forward: it forecasts markets that are open now and places pretend orders against the real prices on offer, paying the fees a real order would pay.
When a market settles, the position is settled too, and the strategy's play-money balance goes up or down.
Because nothing about the future is known yet, paper trading cannot peek at the answer. It is the fairest test a strategy can have short of real money, and nothing here uses real money.
detailed: Orders are filled at the touch (the best ask, or one minus the best bid for the other side) for at most the size resting there, sized by a quarter of the Kelly fraction and capped at 5% of the balance.
The fee is each market's own taker fee, read from the venue with the prices, through the same fee model the backtest uses.
Every cycle, forecast, order and settlement is an entry in an append-only ledger in which each entry's hash covers the previous one, so any edit, deletion or reordering shows.

fees.title: What trading costs
fees.blurb: The fee a buyer pays, and why it matters most at 50–50.
simple: The venue charges a small fee to whoever takes an existing offer. It is largest on a 50–50 market, about 1.25 cents a share on today's sports and weather markets, and shrinks towards nothing as the price nears 0 or 100 cents.
Fees matter because an edge has to be bigger than the fee to be worth anything. Every price and result shown here includes them.
Some older backtests assumed no fees; they say so, because their results would be lower with fees.
detailed: The fee on C shares matched at price p is C · r · (p(1 − p))^e, with the rate r and exponent e published per market in its fee schedule (in 2026: r = 0.05 and e = 1 for sports and weather).
It enters sizing through the effective price a + r(a(1 − a))^e: a trade is taken only if the forecast beats the effective price, not the quoted one.
Makers pay nothing and may receive a rebate; the platform's simulated orders always take, so they always pay.

hard.title: Why beating the market is hard
hard.blurb: The honest benchmark every strategy faces.
simple: The market's price already reflects what many traders know, so a strategy only earns money when it knows something the price does not, by more than the fee.
The sample strategies here are simple on purpose, and none of them beats the market on the markets tested so far. They are the benchmark a new strategy has to clear.
The best forecasters in the world, and the best AI models, find this hard too. That is why every result here is shown next to the market and next to doing nothing.
detailed: On this platform's own backtests (Phase 9) no baseline beat the market: skill was −0.19 for weather climatology, −0.02 for Premier League Elo and −0.12 for Counter-Strike Elo.

On ForecastBench, the Forecasting Research Institute's benchmark, a leading language model (GPT-4.5) scored a Brier of about 0.101 in the October 2025 update, against about 0.081 for superforecasters: a gap of about 0.02.
A two-point Brier edge is also about the smallest a few hundred settled markets can detect; a claimed edge smaller than that, on fewer markets, is indistinguishable from luck.
refs: Karger, E. et al. (2025). ForecastBench: A dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities. ICLR 2025; leaderboard update, Forecasting Research Institute, October 2025.
Project report for Phase 9: live baseline results against the market.

market.name: Market price
market.simple: Uses the market's own chance as its forecast. It never bets, so it is the yardstick the others are measured against.

constant.name: Coin flip
constant.simple: Always says 50–50. It shows what betting with no information does.

elo.name: Team ratings
elo.simple: Rates teams from their past results and bets when its rating disagrees with the price.

climatology.name: Past weather
climatology.simple: Bets on temperatures using how often each one happened on the same dates in earlier years.

llm.name: AI model
llm.simple: Asks a Claude model, which reads evidence from before the forecast, for a chance.

brier.name: Brier score
brier.text: Mean of (forecast − outcome)² over the scored markets. 0 is perfect, 0.25 is what forecasting 0.5 every time earns, 1 is confidently wrong every time. Lower is better.

log.name: Log score
log.text: Mean of −log(probability given to what happened). Punishes confident misses without bound, so forecasts are clipped to [0.01, 0.99]. Lower is better.

skill.name: Skill against the market
skill.text: 1 − (forecaster Brier ÷ market Brier) on the same markets. Positive means the forecaster beat the market price as a forecast, zero equal, negative worse. On paper accounts it is computed from the settled positions so far.

reliability.name: Reliability
reliability.text: Calibration error from the Murphy decomposition: how far each bin's forecasts sit from the frequency that actually happened. Lower is better.

resolution.name: Resolution
resolution.text: How much the forecasts separate outcomes: the spread of observed frequencies across bins around the base rate. Higher is better.

ece.name: Expected calibration error
ece.text: Average absolute gap between forecast and observed frequency across bins, weighted by bin size. Lower is better.

cost.name: Cost
cost.text: Dollars of API usage spent on these forecasts, from token counts at the model's price. Zero for everything but the AI model.

n.name: n
n.text: Markets scored: those every forecaster in the run answered and that had a market price at the cutoff, so all are compared on the same set.

bets.name: Bets
bets.text: Simulated positions placed: one per market where the forecast beat the effective price by at least the minimum edge.

return.name: Return
return.text: Change in the simulated balance over the run, compounding bet by bet in settlement order.

drawdown.name: Max drawdown
drawdown.text: Worst peak-to-trough fall of the balance as a fraction of the peak.

winrate.name: Win rate
winrate.text: Fraction of settled bets that paid out.

pf.name: Profit factor
pf.text: Gross profit divided by gross loss. Above 1 is net profitable.

sharpe.name: Per-bet Sharpe
sharpe.text: Mean per-bet return divided by its standard deviation. Not annualised: bets have no fixed time base.

sharpeci.name: Sharpe 95% interval
sharpeci.text: Bootstrap confidence interval for the per-bet Sharpe ratio. If it includes 0 the edge is not demonstrated.

psharpe.name: P(Sharpe > 0)
psharpe.text: Fraction of bootstrap resamples with a positive Sharpe ratio. Near 0.5 is no evidence of edge; near 1 the edge survived resampling.

cutoff.name: Cutoff
cutoff.text: The moment a forecast is made as of. Every forecaster reads only evidence from before it; in a backtest it is a fixed number of hours before each market settled.

hours.name: Hours before settlement
hours.text: Where the backtest placed the cutoff: this many hours before each market settled.

q.name: Market price q
q.text: The market's price for the first outcome, which is its implied probability; the baseline every forecaster is scored against.

phat.name: Forecast p̂
phat.text: The forecaster's probability that the first outcome occurs.

kind.name: Market type
kind.text: What the question parser read from the question: a match winner, a daily temperature, a season winner, and so on. Forecasters act only on types they understand.

market.name: market (forecaster)
market.text: The market's own price as a forecast. The reference: skill is measured against it and it never bets.

constant.name: constant (forecaster)
constant.text: Always 0.5. A scale anchor: it scores 0.25 Brier by construction, and its bets show what the sizing rule does with no information.

elo.name: elo (forecaster)
elo.text: Elo ratings fitted on results settled before the cutoff, replayed in order from 1500; a home advantage in football; draws from the empirical draw rate.

climatology.name: climatology (forecaster)
climatology.text: For a temperature bucket: how often that bucket happened at the same city on nearby dates in earlier years, from the venue's own resolved markets.

llm.name: llm (forecaster)
llm.text: A Claude model given the question, the cutoff and tools that return evidence from before the cutoff, answering with a probability and a rationale.

ledger.name: Ledger
ledger.text: The append-only record of paper trading: every cycle, forecast, order and settlement, each entry hashed together with the previous one.

verified.name: Chain verified
verified.text: Every ledger entry's hash matches its content and its predecessor, so nothing has been edited, deleted or reordered.

bankroll.name: Balance
bankroll.text: The strategy's paper account: starts at the starting amount and changes with each settled position.

realised.name: Realised
realised.text: Profit and loss from positions that have settled.

exposure.name: Open stake
exposure.text: Money currently tied up in open positions.

fee.name: Fee
fee.text: The venue's taker fee, C · r · (p(1 − p))^e on C shares at price p, with the market's own rate r and exponent e. Included in the effective price and recorded on every paper order.

side.name: Side
side.text: yes buys the first outcome's share; no buys the complementary share, which pays if the first outcome does not happen.

price.name: Price
price.text: Effective price paid per share, fee included. A share pays 1 if its side wins.

shares.name: Shares
shares.text: Number of shares bought: stake ÷ price, capped at the size resting at the touch of the book.

stake.name: Stake
stake.text: Dollars committed, fee included: a fraction of the balance from fractional Kelly, capped at 5% per position.

label.name: Label
label.text: How the market resolved: 1 if the first outcome happened, 0 if not. Set only from the venue's settlement, never from a price.

pnl.name: P&L
pnl.text: Profit or loss of the settled position: shares − stake on a win, −stake on a loss. Net of the fee, which is in the stake.

bid.name: Bid
bid.text: Best resting offer to buy the first outcome's share.

ask.name: Ask
ask.text: Best resting offer to sell the first outcome's share; what a buyer pays before the fee.

minedge.name: Minimum edge
minedge.text: Smallest gap between forecast and effective price worth a bet.

kelly.name: Fractional Kelly
kelly.text: Stake as a fraction of the balance: this multiple of the growth-optimal Kelly fraction, which gives up a little growth for much less drawdown.

spread.name: Half-spread
spread.text: Historical records carry the last price, not the book, so the backtest assumes a bid and ask this far either side of it.

research.title: Research assistant
research.lede: Ask about markets, what was known before a date, or how your strategies have done. It answers only from the data it looks up, and every figure it states is checked against that data before you see it.
research.local_text: The research assistant needs the service and its AI model.
research.label: Your question
research.working: Looking into it; this can take a minute.
research.example_one: Which Counter-Strike series open now are priced between 60 and 85 cents?
research.example_two: How did Arsenal do in their matches before 1 March 2026?

checked.one: The 1 figure in this answer was checked against the data it looked up.
checked.other: All {n} figures in this answer were checked against the data it looked up.

replaced.one: 1 figure could not be found in the data and was replaced by a pointer to it.
replaced.other: {n} figures could not be found in the data and were replaced by a pointer to it.

signals.title: Signals
signals.lede: Tested ways of turning evidence into a chance, each scored against the market's own price on the same settled markets. A signal that beats the market says so here, with how sure that is.
signals.domain_line: {alive} of {n} signals beat the market, {par} cannot be told apart from it, {anti} did worse, and {few} had too few markets to judge; up to {markets} settled markets with a price.
signals.bench_caption: Each signal against the market's price {hours} hours before settlement, on the markets the signal answered: the mean difference in Brier score with a 95% interval (above zero is better than the market), and the markets that difference would need to be told from zero.
signals.reproduce: The same numbers from the same data:
signals.no_bench_text: The bench runs every week on the platform's data.
signals.benchmark_text: Each Monday a set of open markets is frozen and every configuration's forecasts on it are sealed with a fingerprint published at once. When the markets settle, the forecasts are revealed, anyone can check them against their fingerprints, and they are scored. Nothing is ranked below 50 settled questions.
signals.no_weeks: No week has been frozen yet.
signals.week_sealed: {n} questions frozen on {when}; {configs} configurations sealed. Scores appear when the questions settle.
signals.week_scored: {n} questions frozen on {when}; {configs} configurations revealed and scored.
signals.week_hash: Question set fingerprint {hash}, drawn with seed {seed}.
signals.scores_caption: Each configuration on the week's settled questions: Brier score, skill against the market's price at freezing, and whether it has enough questions to be ranked.
signals.reads_price: It reads the market's own price, so it is judged as a correction of it.

comments.title: Comments
comments.note: Your team sees these. Type @ and a teammate's name (the part of their email before the @) to tell them.
comments.deleted: This comment was deleted by its author.
comments.hidden: This comment was hidden by a workspace owner.

team.title: Team
team.lede: Who works in {name} with you, and what has changed.
team.local_text: Teams, notifications and delivery need accounts, which the local view does not have.
team.members_caption: Members of this workspace and their roles
team.leave_confirm: Leave this workspace? You lose access to its strategies and paper accounts until someone invites you again.
team.roles_note: Owners invite people, change roles, connect channels and approve chat senders. Editors make and run strategies. Viewers read and comment.
team.name: Workspace name

action.leaderboard_joined: entered a strategy on the leaderboards
action.leaderboard_left: withdrew a strategy from the leaderboards

team.name_it: This workspace is shared but still called Personal, like everyone's own. Give it a name below so its members can tell it apart.

notifications.title: Notifications
notifications.none: Nothing yet. Mentions, settlements, briefs and warnings appear here.
notifications.where_note: Every notice appears on this page. Tick where else each kind should reach you.
notifications.where_caption: Where each kind of notice is sent besides this page
notifications.quiet_note: Messages that fall in quiet hours wait until they end. This page still shows them at once.
notifications.channels_note: Chats and other destinations are set up under {link}.

leaderboards.title: Leaderboards
leaderboards.lede_simple: Strategies people chose to enter, ranked by how much better their forecasts were than the market's own prices. A strategy is ranked once {n} of its forecasts have settled; before that its lead could be luck.
leaderboards.lede_detailed: Entered strategies ranked by paired Brier advantage over the market price at the same moment, with a 95% bootstrap interval, from paper settlements. Ranking needs {n} settled forecasts. Profit is shown and never ranks.
leaderboards.caption: {domain}, {window}
leaderboards.better: Better than the market, beyond chance
leaderboards.worse: Worse than the market, beyond chance
leaderboards.level: Not distinguishable from the market yet
leaderboards.none_ranked: No strategy has {n} settled forecasts in this period yet.
leaderboards.empty_text: Owners enter a strategy from its page once it is paper trading.
leaderboards.how: Paper trading uses play money. The leaderboards are recomputed every hour from settled paper positions only.

delivery.title: Delivery
delivery.lede_simple: Where research reaches you besides this page, and the briefs sent there on a schedule.
delivery.lede_detailed: Channels, scheduled briefs with their watch lists, signed webhooks, and the read-only tool server for other programs.
delivery.channels_note: A channel is somewhere messages go: an email address, a chat, or a program. People you approve can also ask read-only questions from a chat.
delivery.no_channels: No channels yet. Notices appear on the Notifications page and by email.
delivery.pairing: People asking to use a chat
delivery.pairing_note: Someone new wrote to a chat channel and was given a code. Approve them only if you know who they are: they can then ask questions charged to this workspace's budget.

help.telegram: Create a bot with BotFather, give its token here, and the chat id to post to. You are shown the address to set as the bot's webhook.
help.slack: Create an incoming webhook for the Slack channel. The signing secret lets people in it ask questions; without it the channel only receives.
help.discord: Create a webhook in the Discord channel's settings and paste its URL.
help.webhook: Messages are posted as JSON to this https address.

delivery.inbound: Set this as the chat's webhook address: {url}
delivery.telegram_secret: And this as the webhook's secret token: {token}
delivery.briefs_note: A brief is a short summary sent on a schedule. It lists the same rows the watch list below shows.
delivery.proposed_assistant: Proposed by the assistant; off until you switch it on.
delivery.watch_caption: Watch list from the brief of {date}
delivery.queued: Queued; it arrives in a minute or two.
delivery.webhooks_note: Programs can be told when things happen. Each delivery is signed with the header X-VP-Signature: sha256= and an HMAC of the body under the webhook's secret.
delivery.hook_secret: The webhook's signing secret, shown this once. Keep it where the receiving program can check signatures:
delivery.mcp_note: AI assistants and other programs can read markets, evidence, forecasts, run cards, paper status and the signal bench through a Model Context Protocol server. It has no tool that trades.
delivery.mcp_tokens: Connect with a read token from {link} as a bearer token.

share.title: Share
share.note: A share is a public, read-only page anyone with its link can open. It is a snapshot, refreshed daily, and shows only what you tick.
share.show_spec: Show the rules, so others can copy them
share.board_note: Enter this strategy to be ranked against others by forecasting skill once enough of its paper forecasts have settled.
